source: Google DeepMind blog, Shirobokov, Jaderberg and Babbush, 23 Nov 2026, https://deepmind.google/blog/finding-faster-quantum-algorithms-with-agents-and-formal-verification/: teams of Gemini 4 agents improved well-known quantum algorithms and proved each result in Lean; Lean library, problem specifications and verified solutions open-sourced on GitHub. Cannot test resource-intensive circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, so they are proved mathematically. Fusion (an important property of inertial confinement fusion): 11.8× lower computing cost (qubits and operations combined), memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits. Photochemistry (a common light-sensitive molecule): 8× cheaper. Cytochrome P450 (an enzyme that breaks down most human medicines, important for drug design): 2.5× improvement, memory from 481 to 333 qubits. A specific implementation of Grover's algorithm: 2.57× speedup. Arcsin (a common routine that loads numbers into quantum states): 290×. Running these in scientific simulations would still demand more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide. Paper: Shirobokov et al., “Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI”, arXiv 2611.09822; v1 posted 6 Nov 2026, v2 9 Nov, v3 16 Nov 2026 (the version cited here). Abstract (v3): Gemini 4 agents in a Lean quantum-program library; teams share results through wikis and discuss ideas at organized conferences; improvements vs prior baselines: parallel search up to 2.57×, quantum arithmetic 290×, fusion 12×, photochemistry 8×, drug-metabolism 2.5×. The blog's more precise fusion figure is 11.8×; the Lean cost constants give about 11.81× and about 292× for arcsin (the blog rounds the latter to 290×). Code: https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-quantum-computation, discoveries branch (pinned in the independent review to commit a88de8ff65d78af564b2373088ca369dc95f6547 on 23 Nov 2026). Independent check, SXZ.io, 23 Nov 2026, https://sxz.io/deepmind-quantum-agents-lean-ratios-reproduce-arcsin-260x-refined-baselines-arxiv-versions/: the five headline ratios reproduce from the released Lean files; no custom axioms or native_decide found in a static scan (proofs themselves were not rebuilt). Arcsin (25-bit fixed-point, error at most 1.25e-7): 3,698 T gates on 100 qubits, cost 369,800 qubit·T-gates, vs a published piecewise-polynomial baseline of more than 1.08e8 (245 qubits × 440,576 T gates) whose own error is about 1e-6, above the 1.25e-7 target, described as a lower bound on spacetime cost. Of the ~292× (blog: 290×), 260.1× came from a first kickmix-circuit search stage that classical simulation could check (4,152 T gates on 100 qubits); the Lean-verified second stage cut that to 3,698 T gates, about 1.123× or 11%. A newer inverse-square-root circuit could cut the baseline by up to 3×, leaving at least about 97×; the card follows the paper's chosen baseline and uses “up to about 290 times.” Photochemistry 8× (Lean 8.22×) and P450 2.5× (Lean 2.49×) are against refined baselines that already fold in later literature improvements, not the original published figures (which would read about 11× and 5×). The fusion baseline was not so refined (11.81× against the same published figure). Grover 2.57× is a find-all peak in an oracle-rounds model (find-any peak 1.22×); some fusion and Grover figures changed between arXiv versions (parallel search 1.4× → 2.55× → 2.57×; fusion body 10.9× on 4,374 qubits in v2 → 11.8× on 4,338 in v3). The card follows v3 / the lab post, which match the released Lean constants. Coverage: The New Stack, https://thenewstack.io/deepmind-lean-quantum-verification/, restates the same resource-estimate caveats. Player-facing prose does not name the lab, the model, the proof tool, or the paper. These are proofs about algorithms; no quantum computer ran them. Not stored or shown.
title: Cheaper quantum calculations, proved before a machine can run them
description: Teams of Super Intelligence agents invent new recipes for future quantum computers. A proof-checking program then confirms each recipe is correct and counts how much work it would take, so the savings can be trusted even though no quantum computer has run them. The figures are paper estimates of cost on later machines that can catch their own mistakes.
capability: Super Intelligence agents can now invent cheaper quantum calculations and mathematically prove they work and what they cost, before any quantum computer can run them. The savings are paper estimates, not runs on a real machine.
useCases: The goal: cheaper future quantum simulations that help with fusion reactor design. Named as a hoped-for use; these recipes have not been run on a quantum computer.
The goal: cheaper future quantum simulations of chemistry driven by light, to study how light-sensitive molecules behave. Not run on a quantum computer.
The goal: cheaper future quantum simulations of how the body breaks down medicines, to help with drug design. Not run on a quantum computer.
body:
Usual new recipes for quantum computers are designed by people over years, and the costly ones cannot be tested on today's machines or on ordinary computers. Here, teams of Super Intelligence agents proposed new recipes, shared notes, and met to compare ideas. A proof-checking program then confirmed each recipe does what it should and counted the work it would take on a future quantum computer that can catch its own mistakes.

The largest paper saving was for a common step that loads numbers into a quantum computer: about 370,000 units of cost (100 of the machine's basic information units and 3,698 of a costly kind of operation) against more than 108 million in an earlier published recipe — up to about 290 times lower. That earlier recipe was allowed a slightly looser accuracy target. An independent check found the same ratios, and noted that about 260 times of the gain came from a search stage an ordinary computer could already check, with the proof checker adding about another eleven percent. A fusion-energy simulation was up to about twelve times cheaper (11.8 in the lab post); a light-driven chemistry simulation about eight times cheaper; a simulation of an enzyme that breaks down medicines about two and a half times cheaper; and a well-known parallel search method up to about 2.57 times cheaper. The eightfold and two-and-a-half-fold figures are measured against later, tighter comparison points, not the original published ones. Some fusion and search figures also changed as the paper was revised; this card follows the later figures, which match the released proofs.

These recipes still need more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, and no quantum computer has run them. The proof library, the problem statements and the checked solutions were released publicly.
